blocks.text: Excitatory neurotransmitters generate an action potential in the postsynaptic neuron by making its membrane more permeable to Na+.

blocks.caption: Excitatory neurotransmitters
rows: between motor neurons and skeletal muscle fibres, and between many neurons
made in the CNS and sympathetic nerves; regulates sleep patterns, focus and alertness
released in the adrenal glands and brainstem; a role in sleep, and in becoming and staying alert
in the brain; body movements, pleasure linked to motivation, emotional stimulation
made by neurons of the intestine (about 90%) and CNS (10%); appetite, sleep, memory and learning, temperature, mood, behaviour, muscle contraction

blocks.text: Biogenic amines also act as hormones. Degeneration of dopamine-releasing neurons causes the tremors of Parkinson's disease, and too little activity of serotonin-releasing neurons may cause depression; many antidepressants block the removal of serotonin from the cleft so that it stays there longer.

Inhibitory neurotransmitters lower the chance of an impulse in the postsynaptic neuron. When they bind, chloride channels open instead of sodium channels; Cl- diffuses in and makes the inside even more negative than the RMP. This hyperpolarization inhibits the neuron.

items: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid): the chief inhibitory neurotransmitter of the CNS; it lowers neural excitability, reduces anxiety, stress and fear, and promotes relaxation and sleep. Many sedatives strengthen GABA's binding to its receptors.
Glycine: inhibitory, especially in the spinal cord, brainstem and retina.

Endorphins: released by neurons in the brain; they reduce the release of the excitatory transmitters that carry pain messages, blocking pain signals. Opium and its derivatives morphine and heroin relieve pain because their structure resembles the endorphins and they bind to the same receptors.

blocks.title: Nerve gas
blocks.text: At neuromuscular junctions acetylcholine makes skeletal muscles contract and is then broken down by the enzyme acetylcholinesterase. Nerve gases such as sarin, tabun and soman inhibit this enzyme, so acetylcholine builds up and muscles stay contracted. If the diaphragm stays contracted the person cannot breathe; twitching, convulsions, breathing distress and death can follow.
